planting.note: Sow indoors in late winter and plant out after frost, or transplant nursery-grown divisions in spring into moist, well-drained soil in partial shade.

directions: This evergreen Chilean perennial forms a tidy clump of scalloped, sage-green leaves from which tall, unbranched flower spikes rise in summer, each lined with small dark-veined pale pink flowers that age gracefully on the plant. It tolerates full sun in cool climates but performs best with afternoon shade where summers are hot, and its wiry stems make an excellent, long-lasting cut flower. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor, and deadhead spent spikes to encourage a second flush.

planting.note: Plant divisions into cool, constantly moist, mossy, rocky soil in deep shade near a stream, seep, or waterfall; this species will not tolerate drying out.

directions: Oregon bolandra is a little-grown Pacific Northwest native found wedged into wet, mossy rock crevices and cliff faces along the Columbia River Gorge and the Snake River drainage, where it blooms with loose clusters of small reddish-purple flowers from late spring into summer. In cultivation it wants a cold, humid, constantly wet microhabitat such as a shaded rock garden crevice, streamside boulder, or seep wall rather than ordinary garden soil. It is best suited to native plant and rock garden specialists replicating its narrow natural niche, since it has little tolerance for summer drought or standard border conditions.

planting.note: Plant divisions in gritty, moisture-retentive soil tucked into shaded rock crevices or mossy banks where water seeps; avoid hot, dry sites.

directions: This uncommon saxifrage-family wildflower of the inland Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies grows from slender rhizomes in rocky crevices, ledges, and mossy, shaded seeps, sending up loose clusters of violet (occasionally white) flowers in spring. Its rounded, petiolate leaves form a low rosette well suited to a shaded crevice or trough garden where constant moisture at the roots can be maintained. Because it is rarely offered commercially, propagation is almost always by careful division of established clumps rather than seed, and plants should be sited to mimic its native rocky, perpetually damp habitat.
sources: Montana Field Guide (Montana Natural Heritage Program)

planting.note: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade; established plants tolerate more dryness and heat than most evergreen ferns.

directions: This East Asian woodland fern forms upright, arching clumps of glossy, dark green, heavily veined fronds carried on distinctive dark purple-tinted stipes, slowly spreading from a creeping black rhizome into a patch several feet wide over time. It is notably easy to grow in hot, humid summer climates compared to many evergreen ferns, and tolerates drier shade once established. Use it as a refined, textural evergreen groundcover beneath trees or along a shaded path where its dark stems and glossy foliage read as a deliberate accent rather than a generic fern patch.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden

planting.note: Plant divisions in rich, consistently moist woodland soil in partial to full shade; give it room, as it spreads by long rhizomes and self-sows readily from spores in mild, humid climates.

directions: Native across a broad swath of East and South Asia, this adaptable lady-fern relative forms arching clumps of finely cut, medium-green fronds in average to wet woodland soil, making it one of the easier ferns for beginners in part to full shade. Its chief drawback is vigor: it spreads by creeping rhizomes and produces abundant spores, so in warm, humid regions it is best given a contained bed or a spot where naturalizing is welcome rather than a tight border planting. Pair it with sturdier shrubs that can hold their own against its spreading habit, and avoid siting it near wild areas in frost-free climates where it has shown potential to escape cultivation.

planting.note: Grow in a humid terrarium or greenhouse in bright, indirect light; this tuberous Himalayan species cannot tolerate frost or dry, low-humidity air.

directions: Found on shaded, moist rock ledges and slopes in the Himalayan foothills from Nepal and Sikkim to northeastern India and Myanmar, this small tuberous begonia bears a handful of broadly heart-shaped leaves often blotched with purple, giving rise to its common name. Short stalks of light pink flowers rise just above the foliage before the plant dies back to its tuber during a dry rest period. It needs consistently high humidity and shaded, warm conditions to thrive, making it best suited to terrarium or closed-case cultivation outside the tropics rather than a conventional houseplant setting.

planting.note: Grow in a high-humidity terrarium or greenhouse in a loose, airy, slightly alkaline mix amended with limestone grit; let the surface dry between waterings.

directions: This rhizomatous begonia grows wild wedged into the shaded limestone cliffs and cave mouths of southern China and northern Vietnam, prized in cultivation for its iridescent, silver-flecked leaves that shimmer blue-green in low light. It needs very high ambient humidity, excellent drainage around the roots, and a mineral-rich substrate that mimics its limestone habitat, conditions most reliably provided in a closed terrarium or bioactive vivarium rather than open-air growing. Allow the soil surface to dry slightly between waterings, since this species is prone to rot in constantly soggy mixes.

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or moss-lined wire container in light, rich, well-drained soil in a warm, partly shaded spot; bring indoors well before frost.

directions: A trailing Brazilian species grown for both its small, glossy, heart-shaped leaves and its fragrant white flowers with crimson-splashed throats, which can appear from winter into spring under the right conditions. It is happiest in a moss-lined hanging basket where excellent drainage and airflow around the roots prevent the rot it is prone to when kept too wet. Give it a warm, partly shaded position, pinch new growth regularly to keep it full, and let the soil surface dry before watering again, since this species sulks visibly when overwatered.

planting.note: Plant divisions in damp, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade; confine to a large tub or bed edge where its rapid spread can be managed.

directions: Widely distributed from East Asia to Australasia, this ground fern produces airy, finely divided, light green tripinnate fronds on stipes covered in soft, sticky hairs when young, giving it a lacy texture distinct from coarser creeping ferns. It grows very easily in a damp, dappled-shade position but spreads rapidly by rhizome, so gardeners typically confine it in a large tub or bounded bed rather than letting it run freely among choicer woodland plants. Thin or divide congested patches in spring to keep it in bounds and to propagate new plants for other shaded, damp corners of the garden.

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, well-draining, humus-rich soil in part to full shade beneath trees or large shrubs; mulch to conserve soil moisture.

directions: Native to Australia and New Zealand, this evergreen understory fern forms a neat, dense clump of elegantly divided fronds that read softer and lacier than many larger shield ferns. It thrives as an understory plant beneath taller trees in a naturalistic woodland garden, tolerating a range of shade from dappled to full as long as soil moisture is kept consistent. Maintenance is minimal; simply remove old or damaged fronds as needed and keep mulched to retain the steady moisture this species prefers over its lifetime.

planting.note: Mount on bark or pot in a chunky epiphytic mix in a humid terrarium or greenhouse in filtered shade; water with rainwater or distilled water if tap water is alkaline.

directions: A Central American epiphytic fern with thick, undivided, strap-like fronds covered in fine hairs, grown for its simple, sculptural elephant-ear silhouette rather than typical frilly fern texture. Being purely tropical, it needs constant warmth, high humidity, and acidic water, acclimating gradually from greenhouse half-shade before tolerating any brighter light. It is best mounted on bark or grown in an open, fast-draining epiphytic mix within a closed terrarium or warm greenhouse, since it has no frost tolerance whatsoever.
